payload.body:
@noanflaherty flagging you here since this is the foundation your local-mode unbundling + the Electron IPC tickets (LUM-1997–2000) sit on — wanted to align before more gets built on top.

**What this PR does:** makes `cli/src/lib`'s `hatchLocal`/`retireLocal` (+ the existing guardian-token helpers) consumable in-process — structured return values instead of `void`, an injectable `LifecycleReporter` instead of hard-coded `console.log`, and curated package `exports`. CLI behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged (default console reporter; `HATCH_PROGRESS` contract preserved).

**Why it helps your work:** the Electron main process can now `import { hatchLocal }` and read `{ assistantId, runtimeUrl, guardianAccessToken }` off the return value, instead of the Vite plugin's current approach of spawning the CLI and regex-scraping stdout. So the Electron equivalents of the Vite endpoints become thin adapters over these functions rather than reimplementations.

**What it deliberately does NOT do:** it doesn't add any Electron IPC handler, and it doesn't touch your tickets or the ATL findings — purely additive `cli/`-only groundwork.

Two things I'd like to align on for what happens next:

1. **Who builds the first IPC handler on top of this, and where?** Happy to take a net-new ticket to land one reference adapter (e.g. hatch) over these exports as the pattern for the rest — staying entirely out of your ticket numbers — or leave all of that to you. Your call.
2. **Reporter depth.** The next layer is threading the `LifecycleReporter` through `lib/local.ts` (`startLocalDaemon`/`startGateway`) so an in-process caller observes *all* lifecycle output, not just the top-level lines (see the "Scope boundary" note + Codex thread). That's best validated against the first real consumer — fits naturally with whoever takes on question 1 above.

No coordination blocker either way — this can merge independently and your tickets consume it whenever they're ready. Just want to make sure we're not about to build the same thing twice.

<summary>Architectural observations, drift risks, and small things worth a comment</summary>

## Asymmetry the migration will encounter

`createStorageAccessor` has snapshot caching, `useValue`, and `useSyncExternalStore` integration. `createKeyedStorageAccessor` has none of those — it's a purely imperative `load(id) / save(id) / remove(id)` shape. When LUM-2046 migrates a domain file that wants `useValue(id)`, the answer will be "use createRecordStorageAccessor with a single-entry record" or "lift to createStorageAccessor with key=keyFn(id)" — neither obvious.

Prevents a future contributor from "adding it for symmetry" and re-introducing the snapshot-stability bug.
- Or surface this in LUM-2042's tracking issue so PR C (LUM-2046) considers it when migrating.

Non-blocking either way.

```ts
function set(id, entryKey, value) {
  const existing = load(id);    // parseRecord → JSON.parse + iterate + validate every entry
  existing[entryKey] = value;
  ...
  setLocalSetting(keyFn(id), JSON.stringify(existing));   // re-serialize everything
}
```

Two cases (TTL + LRU) that verify the evictor's sweep skips protected IDs. Both are well-framed and exercise real code paths (not mirrors). The LRU test correctly hacks `lastAccess` via a cast to verify eviction ordering when the oldest entry is protected.

Adding a comment to the effect of "keep this in sync with server.ts" would help the next person.

## Codex P2 — stale parent running on rotated credentials

Codex flagged that after a config reload, a protected parent is marked stale but `injectMessageIntoParent` in `manager.ts` calls `parentConversation.runAgentLoop(...)` directly without checking `isStale()`. This is real: a subagent completion notification could trigger a turn on the old provider/credentials.

That said, this is strictly better than the pre-fix behavior where the parent conversation was *disposed* while the subagent was still running — causing the silent death this PR targets. The stale-provider scenario is a narrower follow-up concern worth a separate ticket. Calling it a blocker here would be holding the fix hostage to a pre-existing gap in a different code path.

Suggested follow-up: guard `injectMessageIntoParent` with `if (parentConversation.isStale()) { /* rebuild or defer */ }` before calling `runAgentLoop`. File as LUM-20xx referencing this PR.

payload.author: devin-ai-integration
payload.body:
Re: Codex review — "Avoid running subagent notifications on stale providers"

This is the pre-existing behavior for all `markStale()` conversations — not a regression introduced by this PR.

When `evictConversationsForReload` fires while a conversation IS processing (line 389–390 before this change), it already calls `markStale()` and the conversation continues its current turn with the old provider/credentials. The next user message triggers `getOrCreateConversation` → `isStale() && !isProcessing()` → rebuild with fresh config.

This PR extends the same `markStale()` treatment to conversations with active subagents. The alternative (current behavior without this fix) is that the parent is evicted immediately, `abortAllForParent` kills all subagents, and the user gets "No subagents found" — a complete failure.

The stale-provider window is narrow: after the subagent notification runs one parent agent loop turn (typically lightweight — the LLM calls `subagent_read`), the next user interaction rebuilds the conversation with fresh config. Routing through `getOrCreateConversation` instead is not viable here because the stale-recreation path calls `abortAllForParent`, which would kill other still-running subagents.

**Value:** This is the right re-scope. The audit caught that the original LUM-1814 prescription would have put server state in Zustand — directly violating `STATE_MANAGEMENT.md`. Surfacing that mid-execution and re-scoping to TanStack Query (with `LUM-2036`/`2037`/`2038` filed for the legitimate Zustand-shaped pieces) is the PR audit philosophy applied to the audit ticket's own scope. The blast-radius discipline — identical external return shape, every consumer untouched — is what makes this safely landable as PR 1 of 4 with the recovery state machine intact for a focused review later (LUM-2038).

<details>
<summary>Architectural observations, load-bearing details, and small drift risks</summary>

## What's been done right

**Retry: false on the query, recovery budget on the hook.** The JSDoc nails the why: TanStack Query retrying on top of `MAX_HATCH_RETRIES` / `MAX_INITIALIZING_RECOVERIES` would burn the budget twice as fast and double-log to Sentry. The mutations stay similarly dumb (no implicit retry) so the recovery state machine stays the single source of truth for hatch+retire concert.

**`refetchInterval` returning `false` for stable phases.** This is exactly the bug `setTimeout`-driven polling makes easy to ship and hard to verify: a tab that never stops polling. The `TRANSIENT_PHASES` set localizes the "when do we keep polling" decision, and the unit tests cover every termination path (active / self_hosted-via-`is_local` / 404 → auto_hatch / 5xx).

**`fetchQuery` in `checkAssistant` instead of direct `getAssistant()`.** The cache-atomic write is the whole point — every other subscriber (sidebar identity, future selectors) sees the same answer the lifecycle path acts on. The old code had `getAssistant()` calls floating around with no shared cache; this was always going to drift.

**Cache-subscribe → re-run `checkAssistant` for side effects.** Polling lands the new value in the cache, the subscribe handler projects it back into the state machine (selfHostedConnection, redirects, assistantId sync). Side effects stay centralized in one function instead of being smeared across the query + the hook.

## Load-bearing detail worth a comment

**The 10s `staleTime` default in `providers.tsx` is what makes the feedback loop terminate.** Here's the chain that almost loops:

1. `refetchInterval` fires → `getAssistant()` runs → cache `"updated"` event.
2. Subscribe handler in `use-assistant-lifecycle.ts` fires → `void checkAssistant()`.
3. `checkAssistant` calls `queryClient.fetchQuery({ queryKey, queryFn })` — *no* explicit `staleTime`.
4. Because the global default is `staleTime: 10_000` and the cache was just written by step 1, `fetchQuery` resolves from cache without firing `queryFn` again. No second cache update. Loop terminates.

If anyone later sets `staleTime: 0` globally — or passes `staleTime: 0` to this `fetchQuery` — every poll completion triggers another `getAssistant()` (deduped, but firing the cache subscriber recursively), and the rate doubles. The comment in `checkAssistant` already says "default behavior is what we want here," but it doesn't call out that "default" means "10s global staleTime." Worth one extra sentence — or better, an explicit `staleTime: POLL_INTERVAL_MS` to make the dependency self-evident at the call site instead of cross-file-implicit.

## Drift risk worth tightening

**`queries.test.ts` re-implements the polling decision instead of importing it.** The production `refetchInterval` callback inlines:
```

```

If someone adds a transient phase to `TRANSIENT_PHASES` (e.g., `pending_restart`), the test stays green against the old behavior. payload.author: vex-assistant-bot
payload.body:
✦ **REQUEST_CHANGES** — reviewed at `3559617b`

**Value:** This is the right re-scope for LUM-1814. Moving the assistant status fetch + polling out of `useAssistantLifecycle` and into a TanStack Query removes the hand-rolled polling timer, gives the result to the query cache (shared across sidebar, identity panel, and any future consumers), and makes the polling policy testable without mocking timers. The fix commit addressed both P1s from my prior review — deps stabilization + fetch-loop prevention — and the overall shape is solid. One new P1 from Codex is blocking.

<details>
<summary>Full analysis</summary>

## Prior P1 fixes — verified ✅

**P1a — mutation dep instability:** `hatchMutation.mutateAsync` / `retireMutation.mutateAsync` are now captured in refs (`hatchMutateRef`, `retireMutateRef`). The `useCallback` dep arrays reference the refs, not the mutation objects, so `hatchAndCheck`, `checkAssistant`, and `recoverStuckInitializingAssistant` identities are stable across renders. The init effect no longer re-fires on every active-user render. ✅

**P1b — cache-subscription fetch loop:** `applyServerStateUpdate` is split out of `checkAssistant`. The cache subscriber now calls `queryClient.getQueryData(...)` + `applyServerStateUpdate()` — zero network calls. `checkAssistant` (which does call `fetchQuery`) is reserved for the visibility-change handler and retry button. The loop is gone. ✅

---

## New Codex P1 — blocking 🔴

**Location:** `hatchAndCheck()` → successful hatch path → `setAssistantState({ kind: "initializing" })`

**Problem:** After a successful hatch, `ASSISTANT_QUERY_KEY` still holds the cached 404 from the initial `/assistant/` fetch. `useAssistantQuery`'s `refetchInterval` is driven by `pollIntervalFor(cachedData)`, which returns `false` for a 404. So `useAssistantQuery` doesn't poll. The cache subscription effect (`lines 566–598`) is now active (because `assistantState.kind === "initializing"`), but it has nothing to observe — no new cache writes are coming in. New users land on the initializing screen and wait until `INITIALIZING_TIMEOUT_MS` fires `recoverStuckInitializingAssistant`.

**Trace:**
```
checkAssistant()           → fetchQuery → 404 → applyServerStateUpdate
  auto_hatch branch        → hatchAndCheck()
    hatch POST 201 ok      → setAssistantState("initializing")
                             // cache still has 404 ← problem
                             // pollIntervalFor(404) = false → no TQ polling
                             // cache subscription active but no writes arriving
→ stuck for INITIALIZING_TIMEOUT_MS (~60s?)
```

**Fix:** Invalidate or seed the cache immediately after a successful hatch so `pollIntervalFor` sees "initializing" status and kicks off the 3s poll:

```ts
// Option A — invalidate (causes one fresh fetch, then poll kicks in)
await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ASSISTANT_QUERY_KEY });

// Option B — seed (skips the redundant re-fetch, directly starts polling)
queryClient.setQueryData<GetAssistantResult>(ASSISTANT_QUERY_KEY, {
  ok: true,
  status: 200,
  data: { ...result.data, status: "initializing" },
});
```

✦ **APPROVE** — reviewed at `f1014c64`

**Value:** Every `addMessage` caller in the daemon no longer needs to count parameter positions or pass `undefined` holes — options are now named, self-documenting, and forward-extensible without a signature break.

**What this does:** Introduces `AddMessageOptions` (daemon-internal) and `InsertMessageOptions` (skill contract), migrates ~20 production call sites and ~252 test call sites, removes the local `InsertMessageFn`/`MessageRole`/`InsertMessageOptions` duplication in `meet-join/conversation-bridge.ts` that was type-casting away real mismatches, and adds a backward-compat IPC shim for version-skew safety.

<details>
<summary>Full analysis</summary>

## Type hierarchy — intentional and correct

The two-type split (`AddMessageOptions` in `conversation-crud.ts` vs `InsertMessageOptions` in `skill-host.ts`) is deliberate:

- `AddMessageOptions` is daemon-internal. It adds `clientMessageId`, the idempotency nonce for daemon-originated inserts (relay, fork, vault repair). Skills have no business setting this.
- `InsertMessageOptions` is the public skill contract. Only `metadata` + `skipIndexing` surface to skills via `SkillHostClient`.
- `addMessage` is structurally assignable to `InsertMessageFn` without a cast now that both sides use options objects — the old `as InsertMessageFn` cast in `daemon-skill-host.ts` is correctly removed.

## Backward-compat IPC shim (`memory.ts` handler)

The handler retains `opts: z.object({ skipIndexing })` in `MemoryAddMessageParams` and resolves `skipIndexing: skipIndexing ?? opts?.skipIndexing`. This correctly covers:
- **New skill → new daemon:** sends flat `{ skipIndexing }`, `opts` is undefined, shim resolves to `skipIndexing`.
- **Old skill → new daemon:** sends `{ opts: { skipIndexing } }`, top-level `skipIndexing` is undefined, shim falls back to `opts.skipIndexing`. ✓

The docstring on `MemoryAddMessageParams` explains the shim rationale ("macOS app and platform do not release together"). Clear and future-maintainable.

## Codex P2 flags — both resolved

**P2 @ `memory.ts:57`** ("preserve opts shape"): The backward-compat shim above handles exactly this. The handler already accepts both shapes. ✓

**P2 @ `client.ts:979`** ("preserve legacy positional args in client"): Devin's rebuttal is correct. `SkillHostClient` is compiled and bundled with the skill binary — an old skill always ships its own old `SkillHostClient` that sends `{ metadata, opts }`. The new `SkillHostClient` only ships with skills rebuilt against the new contract, which use the new options object. The version-skew window is at the IPC wire boundary, handled by the daemon shim. ✓

## `meet-join/conversation-bridge.ts` DRY cleanup

The local `InsertMessageFn` and `MessageRole` redeclarations are gone. The bridge now imports from `@vellumai/skill-host-contracts`, which is the authoritative source. The old local type had a slightly looser return type (`Promise<{ id: string } & Record<string, unknown>>`) vs `Promise<unknown>` in the contract — removing the local copy removes a silent divergence risk.

## `clientMessageId` not forwarded through `SkillHostClient`

`client.ts` sends `{ metadata, skipIndexing }` but not `clientMessageId`. This matches `InsertMessageOptions` (no `clientMessageId` field). Correct — skills shouldn't set client-generated nonces. The IPC handler does accept and forward `clientMessageId` for daemon-internal callers that send it directly.

## CI

20 checks at HEAD: 12 success, 5 skipped (expected: Upload Artifact, Comment Artifact Link, macOS Tests, macOS Build, Lint Unused Code). All substantive checks green. ✓

</details>

payload.body:
✦ **APPROVE** — reviewed at `f7f40be0`

**Value:** Closes the "no unit tests in apps/macos" gap that's been blocking testability of main-process logic. The PR is structured as harness + one proof-of-framework test + explicit follow-up list — exactly the right shape. Trying to land the dock / window-state / index-protocol tests in this PR would have required pre-refactoring three modules to make them testable; landing the harness first means every subsequent file touch can drop in its own test without re-litigating the infra.

<details>
<summary>Architectural choices, design tensions, and small observations</summary>

## What's been thought through well

**Why the `electron` shim exists at all** — `test-setup.ts` mocks the `electron` module because the real module is a native Electron binary and `bun test` runs on plain Linux in CI. Without the shim, any test that transitively imports a `src/main/` file would crash at import time. Shim is intentionally minimal — just enough surface for imports to succeed; per-test specificity is handled via local `mock.module("electron", …)`. This is the right division.

**Why `scripts/run-tests.ts` exists** — Bun's `mock.module()` mutates a process-global registry, so mocks set in one file leak into the next when running `bun test` against multiple files. Subprocess isolation is the documented workaround (linked in the JSDoc). Without this, the `./settings` mock in `commands.test.ts` would silently affect any later test file that imports the same module.

**Why it's a per-package copy of `apps/web/scripts/run-tests.ts`** — Author addresses this directly in the JSDoc: different `cwd`, different `src/` glob (`.ts` vs `.{ts,tsx}`), and the abstraction isn't cheaper than the copy yet. Verified the diff is small (formatting + glob extension + two extra inline comments). Defensible — extraction can wait for the third occurrence.

**Why the follow-ups are deferred, not done here** — `formatBadge`/`computePolicy` are module-private (need an `export`); `restoreBounds` needs per-case `screen.getDisplayMatching` re-mocks; `index-protocol` needs the path-traversal resolver factored into a pure helper. Each is a small refactor that's better landed alongside the test it enables, not bundled into infrastructure. This is the fix-or-surface principle applied correctly: surfaced in the PR body with specifics.

## Codex's catch and the follow-up commit

Codex's P2 on `setPermissionRequestHandler` was real — `src/main/index.ts` calls `session.defaultSession.setPermissionRequestHandler(...)` inside `app.whenReady()`, so any future protocol/index test would have hit `setPermissionRequestHandler is not a function` at import time. Commit `f7f40be0` added both that method and `net.fetch` (also called from `installX` chains). Codex came back clean on re-review. Confirms the shim now covers everything `src/main/index.ts` touches at module evaluation.

## Small things, non-blocking

1. **Bun version drift** — `@types/bun` is `1.3.14`, the CI workflow pins runtime to `1.3.11`. Bun's API surface is stable enough that this is unlikely to bite, but worth keeping in sync the next time either gets bumped.

2. **`TEST_CONCURRENCY=8` default on a 2-core ubuntu-latest runner** — fine because subprocess spawn is cheap, but the interleaved stderr from 8 concurrent failures will be ugly in CI logs. Matches `apps/web/`'s default so consistency wins.

3. **`net.fetch` shim returns an empty `Response`** — anything that depends on the response body would silently pass against this shim. That's by design (tests that exercise `net.fetch` re-mock locally), but worth a sentence in `test-setup.ts`'s JSDoc to make the contract explicit: "import-time stub only; specific behavior is mocked per-test."

4. **`commands.test.ts` mocks `./settings` at module-eval time and dynamic-imports `./commands` after.** Pattern works because the dynamic import resolves after the `mock.module` call. New contributors copying this template should know that order

(2) A 13-line barrel re-export that was actively masking two cross-domain imports is deleted, surfacing the dependencies into the allowlist where the audit tooling can see them.

<details>
<summary>Verification & the Codex/Devin disagreement</summary>

## Moves verified — each really is `utils/`-shaped

For every moved file, checked imports — none reach for a third-party SDK or carry side effects on import:

| File | Imports |
|---|---|
| `utils/api-errors.ts` | (none) — pure error normalization |
| `utils/app-pin-storage.ts` | `@/types/app-types` only |
| `utils/device-settings.ts` | internal types only |
| `utils/initial-message-launch.ts` | (none) |
| `utils/last-viewed-conversation-storage.ts` | (none) |
| `utils/local-settings.ts` | (none) |
| `utils/onboarding-cleanup.ts` | sibling utils only |
| `utils/public-asset.ts` | (none) |

Zero `@/lib/<moved-file>` imports remain anywhere in `apps/web/src/` (checked all nine including `conversations`).

`session-cleanup.ts` JSDoc updated from `lib/device-settings.ts` → `utils/device-settings.ts` to keep the docstring honest.

## The Codex/Devin exchange — partial agreement with both

Codex's concern is real per the CONVENTIONS.md doctrine that "the allow-list shrinks toward zero — don't add new entries by hand; fix the violation instead." This PR adds two entries (`logs/components/logs-tab.tsx → conversations`, `settings/pages/archive-page.tsx → conversations`).

Devin's rebuttal is also right: those imports already existed — `lib/conversations.ts` was a 13-line barrel re-exporting from `domains/conversations/conversation-queries.ts`. The barrel was *hiding* the cross-domain edge from the audit tool, not removing it. So the net effect is:

- **Before:** Two real `logs → conversations` and `settings → conversations` couplings, invisible to the ESLint rule and the audit script
- **After:** Same two couplings, visible in the allowlist, ESLint-enforced, and shows up in `bun run audit:cross-domain`

Visibility-of-dependency is strictly better than barrel-hidden-dependency, even when the count goes up. Codex's deeper point still holds though: the goal-state is a top-level shared seam (probably `hooks/use-conversation-list-query.ts` or similar), and the allowlist growth shouldn't be left as the long-term shape. **Worth confirming LUM-1742 covers that extraction** — if not, a follow-up ticket should track lifting `useConversationListQuery` (plus its `listConversations` + pagination dependencies) up to the cross-domain layer.

Non-blocking for this PR: the move from "hidden + worse" to "explicit + tracked" is the right next step, and the proper extraction is the right step after that.

## Allowlist delta — checked entry by entry

Before (origin/main, 13 files / 15 edges) vs after (this PR, 15 files / 17 edges):
- **+** `src/domains/logs/components/logs-tab.tsx → ["conversations"]` — was barrel-hidden, now explicit
- **+** `src/domains/settings/pages/archive-page.tsx → ["conversations"]` — was barrel-hidden, now explicit

No other allowlist entries added or modified. The two new edges are 1:1 with the barrel's two consumers.

## CI + bots

- 7/7 CI green at `ce0cdcfa` (Lint, Type Check, Build, Test, Socket Security ×2)
- Codex P2: addressed above — non-blocking

payload.author: siddseethepalli
payload.body:
**Heads-up for review (auto-merged via `/do --yolo`)** — risk: low-moderate.

The failing CI job was only the assistant guard test, but the fix also touches the **Swift client** (`clients/shared/Utilities/FeatureFlagRegistry.swift`). That's intentional, not scope creep:

- Commit b32f801b55 added the `both` scope to the registry + TS loader but not the Swift `FeatureFlagScope` enum.
- Swift decodes the bundled registry via `try? JSONDecoder().decode(...)`, so an unknown `both` value fails the **whole** decode → `nil` → the entire client feature-flag registry silently disabled on macOS/iOS.
- So whitelisting `both` in the guard test alone would have turned CI green while leaving a real runtime regression.

**Testing-gap worth a follow-up:** the `CI Main macOS Build & Tests` job stayed green through this regression because no Swift test decodes the *real* bundled `feature-flag-registry.json`. A small Swift test that loads the actual registry and asserts a non-nil decode would catch this class of cross-loader drift — the same role the TS guard test plays.

payload.author: vex-assistant-bot
payload.body:
✦ **APPROVE** — reviewed at `bfa498d5`

**Value:** Treats `STATE_MANAGEMENT.md` as a guide instead of an inventory — removes 114 lines that were duplicating store-by-store details already maintained in source JSDocs. Eliminates a class of doc drift where a file move or refactor silently invalidates the doc; future contributors and agents now find the canonical answer at the call site.

<details>
<summary>Verification</summary>

## Diátaxis fit

The remaining 374 lines map cleanly to the guide/explanation quadrant:
- When to use Zustand vs TanStack Query vs local state
- Store conventions (`State` + `Actions` + `createSelectors`)
- Selector patterns (atomic + legacy `useShallow` migration reference)
- `.use.*` vs `.getState()` API choice
- React Query vs direct SDK
- "No `useReducer`" rule + Flux-inspired direct named actions

What got removed was inventory: which store lives where, what its localStorage keys are, what the current `DEVICE_SETTINGS` registry contains. That's exactly the stuff that goes stale (and would have gone stale today — the `domains/chat/turn-store` paragraph references the post-move path which only landed in #32571 this afternoon).

## Removed content is preserved at the source — verified file by file

| Removed section | New canonical home | Verified |
|---|---|---|
| "Auth state lives in a Zustand store" | `stores/auth-store.ts:1–13` JSDoc | ✅ Covers cross-tab broadcast + foreground re-validation + `getState()` in middleware — actually more thorough than the doc version |
| "Logout destroys the JS context via hard navigation" | `lib/auth/hard-navigate.ts:1–23` JSDoc | ✅ "Logout MUST use this instead of React Router's `navigate()`" — stronger than the removed "Do not replace" wording, and at the call site where the rule actually fires |
| Device-settings table + preserve rule | `lib/auth/session-cleanup.ts:1–22` + `lib/device-settings.ts:1–17` + the `DEVICE_SETTINGS` registry literal | ✅ JSDoc has the "add an entry to DEVICE_SETTINGS" instructions; registry is right below as the source of truth. The doc table was a copy that would have drifted. |
| "Turn state lives in `domains/chat/turn-store.ts`" | `domains/chat/turn-store.ts:1–16` JSDoc | ✅ Covers the phase machine + `getState()` rule + 50ms streaming cadence justification for selectors |
| Terminal-turn cleanup → `endTurn` | `domains/chat/turn-coordinator.ts:1–30` JSDoc | ✅ Two-store-split rationale + the canonical-bug framing + a `reason → action` mapping table — more useful than the prose version |

## Devin's flag — agree with the self-rebuttal

Devin flagged that `"Do not replace hardNavigate() with navigate()"` now lives only in source JSDoc, then commented its own resolution noting it's an intentional trade-off. I agree, with one addition: the JSDoc version (`MUST use this instead of React Router's navigate()`) is **stronger** language than the removed doc text (`Do not replace`), and it lives one line above the function definition — the exact place an agent or contributor would land when touching `hardNavigate()` or its call sites. Discoverability moved *toward* the danger zone, not away from it. Doc-version risk: someone refactors logout, never reads STATE_MANAGEMENT.md, swaps the call. JSDoc-version risk: someone refactors logout, opens the file, sees a 23-line block-comment screaming MUST. The JSDoc placement is better for the failure mode this rule guards against.

## Continuity check

The remaining doc still reads top-to-bottom without orphan references. Transitions at the cut points (after the Zustand-conventions References block; before "Selector patterns") flow cleanly — no dangling "see above" pointers, no broken numbering. Spot-checked all `domains/chat/` and `stores/` path references in the remaining content; all still valid at HEAD.

**Review focus / risk: low–medium** — one architectural decision + one cross-repo dependency.

1. **New `"both"` flag scope (first of its kind).** `home-page` is now the first flag with `scope: "both"`. The backend admits it by widening the scope filter in *both* registry parsers (`gateway/src/feature-flag-defaults.ts`, `assistant/src/config/assistant-feature-flags.ts`) and the loader union/filters (`meta/feature-flags/loader.ts`). The web catalog already supported `"both"` via `scopeIncludes`, so the client still treats `home-page` as a client flag. Nothing else uses `"both"` yet.

2. **Platform companion — please verify (likely no-op).** For the backend to see each user's `home-page` value, the platform must include `home-page` in the remote flag snapshot it pushes to the gateway. Since `home-page` is already provisioned per-user, it is almost certainly already in the snapshot — but worth a quick confirm in `vellum-assistant-platform`. **Failure mode if it isn't:** the resolver falls through to the registry default (`false`) → suppression stays off → conversation is created. That's the safe pre-#32478 behavior (no graveyard cleanup for home-page users until the value flows), not a regression.

3. **Behavior:** suppression now requires `home-page` on. Home-page-**off** installs revert to pre-#32478 behavior (passive notifications create a conversation again). Opt-in (`requiresConversation`) and `reuse_existing` flows are unchanged. Regression test added in `conversation-pairing.test.ts`.
